title: Four dice that beat each other
hook: A usually beats B, B beats C, C beats D. Does A beat D?

doesNotKnow: that 'usually beats' need not chain from one die to the next

misconception: If A usually beats B and B usually beats C, then A beats C.
objective: The learner can explain that 'beats more often than not' need not chain: four dice can each beat the next two times in three, round a loop, so winning is a property of a pair.
keyState: All four matches played: A-B, B-C, C-D (first three seeded 100-roll matches) and the closing D-A, with D winning about two in three.

claims.text: The four dice have faces A: 4,4,4,4,0,0; B: 3,3,3,3,3,3; C: 6,6,2,2,2,2; D: 5,5,5,1,1,1. A match is 100 rolls of both dice and the higher face wins. Stated on the stage as toy dice with no ties.
claims.source: Efron's dice as given in Gardner, Scientific American 223(5): 110-114 (1970); verify the exact faces. No two compared faces tie (enumerated in node). | FACT-CHECK 2026-10-13 (pass 9): Faces match Efron's dice as given by Gardner, 'Mathematical Games: The paradox of the nontransitive dice', Scientific American 223 (December 1970) 110-114 (MathWorld 'Efron's Dice' cites the same). Citation fix for the builder: December 1970 is issue 6, not 5. node: no ties in any of the 4 pairings.

claims.text: A beats B, B beats C, C beats D and D beats A, each in 24 of the 36 face pairs: two in three.
claims.source: Enumeration of 36 face pairs in node, per pair: 24 wins, 0 ties (exactWins() in Demo.tsx; the reveal's '24 in 36' is computed from it). | FACT-CHECK 2026-10-13 (pass 9): node enumeration: AB, BC, CD, DA each 24 wins, 0 ties of 36.

claims.text: The dice averages are 2.67, 3, 3.33, 3, so A has a lower average than B yet beats it, and B beats C although C has the higher average. Averages do not predict who beats whom.
claims.source: mean() in Demo.tsx: A 16/6 = 2.667, B 18/6 = 3, C 20/6 = 3.333, D 18/6 = 3 (node). A beats B 24/36; B beats C 24/36. | FACT-CHECK 2026-10-13 (pass 9): node means 2.667, 3.000, 3.333, 3.000; reveal prints toFixed(2).

claims.text: In the learner's first four matches (shown in the reveal) A beat B 74, B beat C 64, C beat D 75 and D beat A 73 times of 100; rolls of 100 usually land within about ten of 67 (one standard deviation is 4.7), so a result like 57 is ordinary scatter.
claims.source: mulberry32(pair * 1000 + batch + 1), batch 0, pairs in order AB, BC, CD, DA; first seeds tried, untuned (node, same match() as Demo.tsx). Batch 1: 69 69 72 57; batch 2: 60 65 68 64. Binomial sd at p = 2/3, n = 100: 4.7. | FACT-CHECK 2026-10-13 (pass 9): node with own mulberry32 copy and seed pair*1000+batch+1: batch 0 = 74 64 75 73, batch 1 = 69 69 72 57, batch 2 = 60 65 68 64; binomial sd 4.71. · Fact-check pass 19 2026-10-14: Own node with independent mulberry32 and seed pair*1000+batch+1: batch 0 = 74 64 75 73, batch 1 = 69 69 72 57, batch 2 = 60 65 68 64. Binomial(100, 2/3) sd = 4.71; P(57..76) = 0.967 so 'usually within about ten' holds. Note: 57 is about 2 sd low (P(<=57) = 0.028), at the edge of the band; 'ordinary' is fair among the 12 seeded matches but borderline.

claims.text: Winning is a relationship between a pair of dice, not a number a die carries.
claims.source: Follows from c2: the 'beats' relation is a cycle, so no ranking of the dice is consistent with it. | FACT-CHECK 2026-10-13 (pass 9): The cycle A>B>C>D>A (c2) admits no consistent ranking.

recall.question: Die X usually beats Y, and Y usually beats Z. What can you say about X against Z?
options: Nothing for sure: Z can usually beat X, as in a loop of dice
recall.why: 'Usually beats' is a relation between pairs and need not chain. Efron's dice beat each other in a loop, each two times in three.
